The WWR was extreme and unhedged, causing massive CVA losses.
common_traps: Thinking CDS protection has no counterparty risk if the protection seller is rated AAA
Ignoring correlation between reference entity and counterparty when both are financials or both are in the same sector/region
Hedging the market risk of CDS (reference entity spread) but not the CVA/WWR component
questions.real_world_example: In 2007, Bank A bought $5 billion of CDS protection on subprime RMBS from Monoline M. When subprime started defaulting in 2008, Bank A's MTM jumped to +$1.2 billion, but Monoline M's CDS spread blew out from 50 bps to 3000 bps. Bank A faced massive CVA loss (later realized when M was bailed out with haircuts). At 80%+ correlation, the effective protection was worth only 30-40% of par.

questions.question: Compare how collateral mitigates WWR in a structural approach (correlation-based) versus a jump approach (residual value). Why does collateral appear much more effective in the former?
questions.answer_short: In structural approaches, exposure and credit quality evolve gradually through correlation, allowing collateral to be called as exposure increases. In jump approaches, exposure spikes suddenly at default, and collateral cannot adjust during the margin period of risk—making it nearly useless.
questions.answer_long: Figure 17.13 vs Figure 17.14 illustrates this contrast starkly. In a structural/correlation model, as exposure increases, the correlated credit quality deteriorates gradually over days or weeks, triggering collateral calls before default. The collateral actually received is higher in high-WWR scenarios, significantly reducing the collateral-adjusted CVA (slope of CVA vs correlation is much flatter with collateral). However, in a jump model like the FX residual value approach, the FX rate jumps by 20-40% instantaneously at default. No collateral call can occur during this jump—the margin period of risk doesn't help because there is no 'period' of gradual exposure increase. The collateralized exposure cannot go below the jump size (20% in Figure 17.14), so collateral is nearly ineffective. The truth for real counterparties lies somewhere between: some systemic counterparties (banks, sovereigns) exhibit jump-like behavior, while non-systemic counterparties (corporates) may deteriorate more gradually.
questions.why_it_matters: This tells you that collateral is most effective as a WWR mitigant for non-systemic counterparties and least effective for systemic ones. Ironically, banks (highly systemic) are the main users of collateral, while corporates (less systemic) often post none. CCPs, which rely entirely on collateral, are therefore most vulnerable to WWR precisely from their systemic clearing members.
common_traps: Assuming collateral always reduces WWR proportionally to how it reduces normal exposure
Using correlation models to justify thin initial margins for systemic counterparties
Ignoring that margin period of risk is much less helpful when jumps are involved
questions.real_world_example: Lehman Brothers posted collateral to many counterparties under daily-margined CSAs. Yet when Lehman defaulted in September 2008, many counterparties still suffered losses despite holding collateral. Why? Because Lehman's default was accompanied by a market dislocation (CDS spreads, equity volatility, funding spreads all jumped simultaneously). The exposure increase happened faster than the margin period of risk, and in some cases the collateral itself (Lehman bonds) was wrong-way collateral.

questions.question: Why are CCPs particularly vulnerable to WWR, and what is the 'CDO analogy' for CCP default waterfalls? What perverse incentive does this create?
questions.answer_short: CCPs separate credit quality from exposure, charging margins based mainly on market risk. This ignores that high-quality members create more severe WWR (larger conditional exposure given default). The CCP waterfall resembles a CDO where members hold the 'super-senior' risk, which is concentrated in systemic tail events.
questions.answer_long: CCPs face WWR because they: (1) require minimum credit standards for members but don't scale margins by credit quality; (2) rely heavily on initial margin and default funds calibrated to exposure/VaR, which may not capture WWR; (3) admit large, high-quality banks as members, who create the most severe WWR per Figure 17.2 and Table 17.2 (better credits = bigger surprise defaults = larger conditional exposures). The CDO analogy from Figure 17.15 shows that initial margin and the defaulter's default fund contribution form the 'first loss' piece, while surviving members' default fund contributions and loss mutualization represent the 'super-senior' tranche. This senior piece is supposedly safe (low probability) but is highly concentrated in systemic risk—it pays out only when a major member defaults in extreme market conditions. Perversely, this suggests CCPs should charge higher margins to stronger credits, but doing so would be economically and politically difficult.
questions.why_it_matters: CCP resilience is critical for financial stability, but their WWR vulnerability is underappreciated. If a large clearing member defaults during a severe crisis (high WWR scenario), the CCP may exhaust defaulter-pays resources and require loss mutualization among survivors, potentially creating a cascade of failures. The 2018 Nasdaq Clearing default of member ABN AMRO Clearing showed how quickly margins and default funds can be exhausted.
common_traps: Assuming CCPs are 'too big to fail' and therefore don't need to manage WWR carefully
Thinking that high initial margins automatically solve WWR (they don't if WWR is jump-based or involves collateral quality issues)
Believing diversification across many clearing members eliminates WWR (systemic events can hit many members simultaneously)
questions.real_world_example: During March 2020 COVID crisis, LCH (a major rates CCP) faced simultaneous margin calls on hundreds of clearing members as interest rate volatility spiked. Several large members were stressed, and there was concern about a potential default. If a Tier-1 bank had defaulted, the WWR would have been severe: their derivatives exposure would have been massive (due to market dislocation), and margin collected might have been insufficient despite the extreme moves. Other clearing members would have faced billions in assessments, potentially triggering secondary defaults.

questions.question: Why is historical data often uninformative for calibrating WWR models? Give an example where correlation appears zero historically but severe WWR exists.
questions.answer_short: WWR is often a tail event or structural relationship that doesn't appear in normal times. Historical correlation can be zero because the default or crisis hasn't happened yet. Example: EUR/sovereign credit correlation was near zero pre-2010 but became strongly negative during the 2011-2012 crisis.
questions.answer_long: Historical data fails for WWR because: (1) Defaults are rare, so you have few data points in the tail where WWR matters; (2) WWR may be caused by structural linkages that only activate in stress (e.g., a corporate posts its own bonds as collateral—in normal times this seems fine, but in default it's worthless); (3) Correlations measured in normal times may not hold in crises due to regime shifts. The classic example is European sovereigns pre-2010: analyzing 2000-2009 data showed very low correlation between EUR exchange rate and sovereign credit spreads because there were no sovereign defaults or near-defaults. A model calibrated to this data would show zero WWR. Yet in 2010-2012, the relationship became strongly negative—as sovereign spreads blew out, the EUR weakened. Zero historical correlation did not mean zero dependency; it meant the stress scenario hadn't occurred yet.
questions.why_it_matters: This is why stress testing and scenario analysis are critical complements to statistical modeling of WWR. You cannot rely solely on historical calibration—you must use economic reasoning and hypothetical scenarios to identify and quantify WWR that hasn't yet manifested in data.
common_traps: Trusting that zero historical correlation means no WWR (correlation ≠ independence)
Using only 'normal times' data to calibrate WWR models without stress-period data
Dismissing WWR concerns because 'we've traded with this counterparty for years with no issues'
questions.real_world_example: Many banks traded actively with Icelandic banks in the 2000s. Historical data showed Icelandic banks were stable and the króna was fairly stable. Correlation analysis suggested little WWR. Then in 2008, all three major Icelandic banks defaulted simultaneously and the króna crashed by 50%+ in weeks. Any FX forward or cross-currency swap exposure to these banks suffered extreme losses that historical models completely missed.

questions.question: Your bank's CVA desk identifies a potential specific WWR trade: buying a 10-year put option on Spanish bank BBVA stock from another Spanish bank, Santander. What actions should you take before approving this trade?
questions.answer_short: This is severe specific WWR and should likely be avoided entirely or require substantial mitigants: demanding high-quality collateral (not Spanish assets), significantly widening CVA charge, requiring explicit senior management approval, or finding an alternative counterparty with weaker correlation to BBVA.
questions.answer_long: Specific WWR should be addressed qualitatively through risk policies, not just priced quantitatively. Actions: (1) Quantify the WWR—both BBVA and Santander are Spanish banks, highly correlated (likely 70%+ credit correlation); the put is valuable only when Spanish banking sector is stressed, precisely when Santander is most likely to default. (2) Calculate CVA with high correlation assumptions (60-80%) and potentially add a WWR buffer. (3) Require senior approval as this violates best practices for specific WWR. (4) Demand strong mitigation: collateral must be non-Spanish high-quality assets with very conservative haircuts, or a credit support annex with a low threshold. (5) Consider alternative execution—hedge with a non-Spanish counterparty or exchange-trade the option. (6) If trade proceeds, actively hedge both the market risk (BBVA stock price) and the CVA (Santander credit spread), but recognize the hedge will be imperfect due to correlation risk.
questions.why_it_matters: Specific WWR trades were at the heart of 2008 losses. Banks bought CDS protection from monolines on assets highly correlated with the monolines' own portfolios (subprime RMBS). Regulators now expect banks to identify and avoid specific WWR or impose stringent controls. Basel III explicitly requires additional capital for WWR in the standardized approach.
common_traps: Approving the trade just because the CVA charge is 'fairly priced' (some trades should not be done at any price)
Assuming collateral fully mitigates the risk (if Santander defaults in a Spanish banking crisis, even Spanish government bonds may be impaired)
Relying on diversification across the portfolio to offset this concentrated risk
questions.real_world_example: In 2008-2011, many banks bought CDS protection on Greek sovereign debt from Greek banks (Alpha Bank, National Bank of Greece). When Greece restructured in 2012, these banks were simultaneously insolvent, and the protection was nearly worthless. Banks that had priced the WWR and avoided these counterparties or demanded cash collateral in non-Greek currency fared much better.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between general wrong-way risk and specific wrong-way risk?
questions.answer_short: General WWR arises from macro-economic relationships detectable in historical data, while specific WWR arises from structural/causal linkages between exposure and default that often aren't captured in market experience.
questions.answer_long: General WWR is based on broad macro-economic behavior patterns that can potentially be detected using historical correlations (like interest rates falling during recessions when defaults increase). Specific WWR stems from direct structural relationships between the transaction, counterparty, and market that create cause-and-effect dependencies. Specific WWR is harder to detect except through understanding the economic rationale behind transactions and may be extreme enough to warrant avoidance rather than just pricing.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this distinction is critical for risk management: general WWR can be priced using correlation models, while specific WWR may be so severe it should be avoided entirely through transaction restrictions or addressed qualitatively via stress-testing.
common_traps: Assuming all WWR can be captured by historical correlation analysis
Treating specific WWR as just 'high correlation' general WWR
Believing that zero historical correlation proves independence
questions.real_world_example: During the 2010 European sovereign crisis, the euro weakened as sovereign credit deteriorated - a relationship not evident in historical data because these sovereigns had never previously faced such stress. This was specific WWR that historical correlations completely missed.

questions.question: Why does a receiver interest rate swap with a corporate counterparty typically exhibit wrong-way risk?
questions.answer_short: When a corporate pays floating and receives fixed, the swap is valuable to them when rates fall - but rates typically fall during recessions when corporate default probability increases.
questions.answer_long: In a receiver swap, the bank receives floating and pays fixed to the corporate. The exposure to the bank (positive MTM) occurs when interest rates fall below the fixed rate. However, interest rates typically decline during economic recessions due to central bank intervention, which is precisely when corporate default rates increase. This creates an adverse dependency where exposure is high when default probability is also high, creating WWR for the bank.
questions.why_it_matters: This is one of the most common WWR scenarios banks face, especially with uncollateralized corporate counterparties, and was a major source of unexpected CVA losses during the financial crisis when receiver swaps moved deeply in-the-money as counterparty credit deteriorated.
common_traps: Assuming WWR only matters at default rather than during credit deterioration
Ignoring that interest rates can rise during stress (though this is less common)
Thinking collateral completely eliminates this WWR if it's posted gradually
questions.real_world_example: During 2008-2009, banks holding uncollateralized receiver swaps with corporates and sovereigns saw both massive increases in MTM (as rates were cut to near zero) and severe credit deterioration, creating significant WWR-driven CVA losses.

questions.question: How is wrong-way risk incorporated into the CVA calculation formula, and what does the conditional exposure term represent?
questions.answer_short: WWR is incorporated by using conditional expected exposure: CVA = LGD × Σ EE(ti | ti = τC) × PD(ti-1, ti), where EE is conditioned on the counterparty defaulting at that time.
questions.answer_long: The standard CVA formula uses unconditional expected exposure, implicitly assuming independence between exposure and default probability. To incorporate WWR, we replace EE(ti) with EE(ti | ti = τC), the expected exposure conditional on counterparty default occurring at time ti. This conditional exposure will be higher than unconditional exposure when WWR exists, because we're only looking at scenarios where default actually happens - which tend to be scenarios where exposure is higher due to the adverse correlation.
questions.why_it_matters: This is the mathematically correct way to calculate CVA with WWR. Understanding this formula helps practitioners see that WWR increases CVA by increasing the exposure used in the calculation, not by changing the default probability component.
common_traps: Trying to adjust default probabilities instead of exposure to capture WWR
Thinking conditional exposure is always higher (it could be lower with right-way risk)
Confusing conditional expectation with simple scenario analysis
questions.real_world_example: For an FX forward with a weak-currency counterparty, the conditional exposure EE(t|default at t) might be 50% higher than unconditional EE(t) if the currency typically jumps 30% weaker at sovereign default, dramatically increasing CVA.

questions.question: Why does wrong-way risk exposure actually increase as the counterparty's credit quality improves, and what is the intuition behind this counterintuitive result?
questions.answer_short: Better credit quality means default is more surprising and unexpected, so when it does occur, it represents a bigger adverse shock that coincides with more extreme market moves, increasing conditional exposure.
questions.answer_long: For a high-quality counterparty, default is a very low probability event. When such an unlikely event actually occurs, it must be associated with an extreme market scenario - a 'tail event' that required something very bad to happen. In contrast, for a weak counterparty, default is more expected and can occur in more ordinary market conditions. Therefore, the conditional exposure given default of a strong counterparty tends to be higher than for a weak counterparty, because the default itself signals more extreme market stress when WWR correlations exist.
questions.why_it_matters: This has profound implications for risk management: WWR is actually more dangerous with high-quality counterparties like AAA sovereigns. This explains why Greek sovereign default had more severe FX and market impacts than defaults of lower-rated emerging market sovereigns.
common_traps: Assuming WWR is worse for weak credits because they default more often
Ignoring the 'conditional on default' aspect of the calculation
Thinking better credit quality always means lower counterparty risk in all dimensions
questions.real_world_example: The Levy and Levin (1999) study showed AAA sovereign defaults had 17% currency residual value versus 62% for CCC, meaning the currency jump was much larger for higher-rated sovereigns - validating this theoretical prediction with empirical data.

questions.question: Explain how a cross-currency swap can exhibit wrong-way collateral risk, and why this cannot be completely eliminated even with daily margining.
questions.answer_short: If collateral is posted in one of the swap currencies, an adverse FX move simultaneously increases exposure while devaluing the collateral. The margin period of risk prevents immediate re-margining, leaving residual exposure.
questions.answer_long: Consider a USD/EUR cross-currency swap where the counterparty posts EUR cash as collateral. If EUR weakens dramatically, the swap's value to you (in USD terms) increases as you're receiving the now-stronger USD leg. However, simultaneously, the EUR collateral you're holding loses value in USD terms. Even with daily margining, the margin period of risk (typically 10 business days for bilateral, longer for disputes) means you cannot instantly call for additional collateral or liquidate and re-hedge. During this period, the FX rate can move further, creating uncollateralized exposure precisely when counterparty credit may also be deteriorating.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a practical problem for any cross-currency trading with cash collateral in one of the currencies. The book shows this can increase exposure by ~50% versus currency-independent collateral, significantly impacting CVA calculations and capital requirements.
common_traps: Thinking daily margining eliminates all collateral WWR
Ignoring the currency denomination of collateral in exposure calculations
Assuming the margin period of risk is negligible for FX moves
questions.real_world_example: During the 2010-2012 Eurozone crisis, banks holding cross-currency swaps collateralized with EUR faced exactly this problem - as counterparty credit deteriorated, EUR weakened, simultaneously increasing exposure and reducing collateral value.

questions.question: What is the main limitation of the hazard rate approach to modeling WWR, and why does it typically generate only weak dependency effects?
questions.answer_short: Hazard rate models generate WWR by correlating stochastic credit spreads with market risk factors, but this only captures gradual, continuous relationships and produces weak effects even at very high correlations.
questions.answer_long: The hazard rate approach models credit spreads as a stochastic process (like lognormal) and correlates it with other market variables (interest rates, FX, etc.). Default is then triggered when the integrated hazard rate reaches a threshold. However, this approach can only capture smooth, continuous relationships between variables. Even with -90% correlation between interest rates and credit spreads, the resulting conditional exposure increase is modest. The approach misses structural breaks, jumps at default, and cause-and-effect relationships that create severe specific WWR. It essentially only captures gentle macro-economic drift effects.
questions.why_it_matters: Practitioners need to understand that hazard rate models, while mathematically tractable and easy to implement using existing simulation infrastructure, will systematically underestimate WWR in many situations, particularly those involving specific WWR or jump-to-default scenarios.
common_traps: Thinking high correlation parameters will capture all WWR effects
Using hazard rate approaches for products with jump risks like sovereign FX
Calibrating to historical correlations without considering structural breaks
questions.real_world_example: The book shows that even with -90% correlation in a hazard rate model for an interest rate swap, the WWR effect is 'not particularly strong' - far less than what structural or jump models would predict for the same economic scenario.

questions.question: How does the structural approach to WWR modeling differ from the hazard rate approach, and what is its key advantage and disadvantage?
questions.answer_short: The structural approach maps pre-computed exposure distributions and default times onto a bivariate distribution, avoiding resimulation. The advantage is computational efficiency; the disadvantage is an opaque correlation parameter that's hard to calibrate.
questions.answer_long: Unlike hazard rate approaches that simulate credit and market variables jointly, the structural approach takes existing unconditional exposure distributions and maps them (along with the default time distribution) onto a bivariate copula structure. This creates dependency without resimulating anything. The advantage is that you can layer WWR onto existing CVA infrastructure without recalculating exposures. However, the correlation parameter in the bivariate distribution is abstract and not directly observable in markets, making calibration difficult. It's also unclear whether all relevant WWR information is truly contained in the unconditional exposure distribution.
questions.why_it_matters: Many banks use structural approaches because they're computationally cheap and can be 'bolted on' to existing CVA engines. However, the calibration difficulty means the correlation parameter often becomes a subjective risk management assumption rather than a market-calibrated input.
common_traps: Thinking the correlation parameter is the same as asset correlation or credit spread correlation
Assuming unconditional exposure contains all information needed for WWR
Using arbitrary correlation values without economic justification
questions.real_world_example: A bank might calculate standard CVA with unconditional exposures, then apply a structural model with +25% correlation as a 'WWR adjustment' to get regulatory capital approval, but struggle to justify why 25% rather than 50% is appropriate.

questions.question: What is the Hull-White parametric approach to WWR, and how does calibration differ from the structural approach?
questions.answer_short: Hull-White links default probability directly to portfolio value through a simple functional relationship with parameter b, calibrated either via historical value/spread relationships or what-if scenario analysis.
questions.answer_long: The Hull-White approach creates a parametric function where default probability depends directly on the current portfolio MTM, controlled by a single parameter b. Unlike the structural approach's opaque correlation, b can be calibrated by examining historical relationships: calculate the portfolio's historical values and compare with the counterparty's credit spreads over time. A strong positive relationship indicates WWR. Alternatively, b can be calibrated to match a specific scenario (e.g., 'if portfolio moves to 95th percentile MTM, what should credit spread be?'). This makes calibration more intuitive and grounded in observable data.
questions.why_it_matters: The calibration advantage makes this approach more defensible for regulatory purposes and internal risk management. Being able to point to historical data relationships or stress scenarios makes the WWR adjustment less arbitrary than abstract correlation parameters.
common_traps: Assuming current portfolio composition matches the historical portfolio used for calibration
Forgetting that historical relationships may not hold in crisis (regime shift)
Overlooking that the approach requires a stable, similar portfolio over time
questions.real_world_example: A bank trading interest rate swaps with a corporate could calibrate b by looking at how their swap portfolio MTM moved relative to the corporate's CDS spread over the past 3 years, establishing an empirical WWR relationship for pricing new trades.

questions.question: Explain the devaluation/jump approach for FX wrong-way risk using residual value (RV) factors, and why the impact is approximately time-homogeneous.
questions.answer_short: The approach assumes the FX rate jumps by (1-RV) at counterparty default, where RV is the residual currency value. This creates similar percentage exposure increases across all maturities since the jump is proportional to current exposure.
questions.answer_long: Based on Levy and Levin's empirical work, when a sovereign defaults, their currency typically devalues suddenly by an amount (1-RV), where RV might be 17% for AAA or 62% for CCC. At the moment of default, all FX exposures jump by this factor. This impact is time-homogeneous because the jump is proportional - a 1-year forward and 10-year forward both see their exposure increase by the same percentage. The conditional exposure shown in Figure 17.11 is approximately parallel to the unconditional profile. This is supported by CDS market evidence (Table 17.3) showing similar quanto effects across maturities.
questions.why_it_matters: This is the standard approach for pricing sovereign FX trades and explains why banks charge significant CVA on such transactions. The approach is also validated by quanto CDS spreads, which reveal market-implied RV factors and confirm the time-homogeneous assumption.
common_traps: Thinking the jump happens gradually and can be collateralized
Assuming RV is the same for different counterparty types (sovereign vs. corporate)
Using RV calibrated to historical defaults without adjusting for current crisis probability
questions.real_world_example: In April 2011, Italian CDS quoted at 131 bps in USD but only 91 bps in EUR, implying a 69% residual value of the euro in the event of Italian default - this RV factor would be used to price FX trades with Italian counterparties.

questions.question: How do quanto CDS spreads (same credit event, different payment currencies) provide market evidence for WWR jump assumptions, and what do they reveal about credit quality effects?
questions.answer_short: Quanto CDS show that USD-denominated protection costs more than local-currency protection on the same reference entity, revealing the market-implied currency jump at default. Higher-rated credits show stronger quanto effects.
questions.answer_long: When the same CDS is quoted in USD versus local currency (e.g., EUR for European sovereigns), they should trigger on identical credit events. The only difference is payment currency on default. If USD CDS costs 131 bps but EUR CDS costs 91 bps (Italian example), this 40 bps difference reflects the market's expectation that EUR will be worth less at Italian default time - implying RV ≈ 69%. The fact that this quanto spread exists and persists provides direct market evidence for jump-at-default assumptions. Moreover, the book shows Germany (75% RV), Spain (80%), Italy (83%) and Greece (91%) - better-rated sovereigns have lower RV, meaning bigger expected jumps, confirming the credit quality paradox.
questions.why_it_matters: Quanto CDS provide the rare case where WWR effects are directly observable and tradeable in markets, allowing genuine market calibration rather than model assumptions. They also offer potential WWR hedging instruments.
common_traps: Forgetting to adjust for FX forwards and cross-currency basis in calculating implied RV
Assuming quanto spreads are pure WWR without considering other factors
Thinking quanto CDS are widely liquid (they're often quite illiquid)
questions.real_world_example: During the peak of Eurozone crisis in 2011, implied RVs from quanto CDS were 91% for Greece and 75% for Germany, meaning markets expected a 25% euro devaluation if Germany defaulted versus 9% for Greece - counterintuitive but consistent with default being more surprising for better credits.

questions.question: For a CDS where you are buying protection, why does the fair premium drop to approximately the recovery rate at 100% correlation with the reference entity, and what does this reveal about CVA magnitude?
questions.answer_short: At 100% correlation, the protection seller always defaults when the reference entity defaults, so you only receive the recovery value (not par), making the CDS worth only recovery × spread = 40% × 250 bps = 100 bps.
questions.answer_long: When buying protection via CDS, you pay a premium and expect to receive (1-LGD) × notional if default occurs. However, if the protection seller has 100% correlation with the reference entity, they default simultaneously. In this case, you only receive the recovery value of the protection seller's obligation, which is (1-LGD) on your claim. This means the CDS is only worth (1-LGD) of its face value. If the reference entity CDS should trade at 250 bps with no counterparty risk, at 100% correlation you would only pay approximately 0.4 × 250 = 100 bps (assuming 60% LGD). The CVA is therefore 150 bps or 60% of the premium - massive!
questions.why_it_matters: This demonstrates that CDS counterparty risk can dwarf the actual credit risk being hedged when correlation is high. It explains why buying protection from a bank on their own sovereign is nearly worthless, and why monoline insurance companies holding highly correlated credit portfolios created such massive CVA exposures.
common_traps: Thinking CDS counterparty risk is small because spreads are low
Ignoring that protection becomes worthless at high correlation even before 100%
Assuming collateral will save you (monoline/CDPC experience proved otherwise)
questions.real_world_example: During the financial crisis, buying CDS protection from banks on financial reference entities or their sovereigns proved nearly worthless, with protection buyers suffering massive losses when both protection seller and reference entity deteriorated together - some banks had CVA on CDS books exceeding 50% of notional.

questions.question: Why do hazard rate/structural approaches suggest collateral is effective against WWR while jump approaches suggest it is nearly useless, and which view is more realistic?
questions.answer_short: Hazard rate/structural models show gradual exposure increases that can be collateralized as they develop. Jump models show sudden exposure spikes at default that cannot be margined. Reality depends on whether WWR manifests gradually or via jumps.
questions.answer_long: Hazard rate and structural approaches model WWR as smooth, continuous correlation effects. As exposure gradually increases (along with credit deterioration), the counterparty can post additional collateral over days/weeks, effectively mitigating most WWR. However, jump approaches (like FX devaluation) assume exposure spikes suddenly at default time - the FX rate jumps 30% the instant the sovereign defaults. No amount of daily margining can prevent this, leaving exposure at the full jump amount. The truth likely lies in between: for systemic counterparties (large banks, sovereigns), jumps dominate due to market dislocations at default. For smaller counterparties, gradual deterioration is more likely, making collateral more effective.
questions.why_it_matters: This fundamentally affects how much credit you give collateral for mitigating WWR in CVA calculations and capital models. Pykhtin and Sokol (2013) show banks (systemic) should get less collateral benefit than corporates (non-systemic) - but banks are the ones who actually post collateral!
common_traps: Assuming daily margining means collateral eliminates all WWR
Using hazard rate models for products with obvious jump risk
Ignoring that margin period of risk extends during market stress/defaults
questions.real_world_example: Lehman's default created immediate jumps in CDS spreads, FX rates, and equity prices that far exceeded any plausible margin call, leaving counterparties with massive uncollateralized exposures despite having CSAs. The 'jump' view proved correct for systemic defaults.

questions.question: Why are CCPs particularly vulnerable to wrong-way risk despite their reliance on collateral, and how does the 'credit quality paradox' affect CCP margining?
questions.answer_short: CCPs separate credit assessment from margin calculations, ignoring that better credit quality members create more WWR. They also face jump risks where collateral is ineffective, yet charge margins based mainly on market risk.
questions.answer_long: CCPs determine membership based on credit quality but then charge initial margins and default fund contributions driven primarily by portfolio market risk (volatility, VaR). This ignores the WWR credit quality paradox: better members (large banks) create more severe WWR because their default is more surprising and more systemic, causing larger market dislocations. Additionally, CCPs clearing CDS or FX face jump-at-default risks where collateral posted based on recent volatility proves inadequate when a member defaults. Perversely, optimal CCP design would charge MORE margin to better credit quality members, which is politically and practically difficult.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a fundamental design flaw in CCPs that became apparent in discussions of CDS clearing. If a major bank clearing member defaults, the CCP faces massive WWR that margins calculated from normal market conditions won't cover, potentially exhausting the waterfall and imposing losses on surviving members.
common_traps: Thinking CCPs have solved counterparty risk through collateralization
Assuming stronger clearing members always mean safer CCPs
Ignoring that CCP loss waterfalls concentrate systemic risk in senior tranches
questions.real_world_example: If JP Morgan defaulted as a CCP clearing member, the resulting market dislocations would likely dwarf the initial margins held, because margins are calibrated to normal volatility not jump-to-default scenarios - creating massive losses that would flow through the waterfall to other members.

questions.question: Explain the analogy between a CCP loss waterfall and a CDO structure, and why this implies clearing members have exposure to concentrated systemic risk.
questions.answer_short: The defaulting member's IM and default fund are 'first loss', CCP equity is mezzanine, and surviving members' default funds are 'second loss' - which acts like a senior CDO tranche heavily concentrated in systemic tail risk.
questions.answer_long: In a CDO, first loss tranches absorb initial defaults (like defaulting member's initial margin and default fund contribution), mezzanine takes intermediate losses (CCP equity), and senior tranches only lose in catastrophic scenarios (surviving members' default funds and assessments). Clearing members therefore hold implicit senior tranche exposure on an unknown, constantly changing synthetic CDO. Senior tranches are well-known to have extreme concentration in systemic tail risk - they either lose nothing (most likely) or lose heavily (rare but severe). This means clearing members are exposed not to diversified counterparty risk but to concentrated 'all banks fail together' scenarios, exactly when their own financial health is also deteriorating (WWR at the member level!).
questions.why_it_matters: This reveals that CCP membership is not a diversified, mutualized risk but rather a concentrated bet on systemic stability. During a crisis, your default fund contribution is most likely to be called exactly when you can least afford it, and the magnitude could be enormous if multiple members fail.
common_traps: Thinking default fund contributions are like insurance premiums (capped losses)
Assuming CCP mutualization means diversification (it creates concentration)
Ignoring that assessments can exceed committed default fund amounts
questions.real_world_example: If multiple European banks defaulted as CCP clearing members during a sovereign crisis (high correlation scenario), the surviving members' default fund exposure would behave like a senior tranche - losing heavily in exactly this systemic scenario. This is why Gibson (2004), Coval et al. (2009) showed senior tranches are most exposed to systemic risk despite being 'senior'.

questions.question: How does adverse selection in collateral posting create additional wrong-way risk for CCPs, and why is this problem worse than for bilateral counterparties?
questions.answer_short: Clearing members will optimally post the riskiest eligible collateral (highest WWR relative to haircut). Unlike bilateral counterparties, CCPs face political pressure to accept wide asset ranges but can't negotiate member-specific terms, concentrating risky collateral.
questions.answer_long: When CCPs accept a broad range of collateral to attract members and provide flexibility, clearing members will naturally post assets with the highest risk-adjusted 'value' - meaning assets where the CCP's haircut underprices the true risk, especially WWR. For example, a European bank will preferentially post Italian BTPs if the haircut is 10% but the WWR jump risk is 20%. This adverse selection means CCPs accumulate precisely the collateral most likely to fail when members default. Unlike bilateral relationships where collateral can be negotiated counterparty-by-counterparty, CCPs have uniform rules making adverse selection systematic. While CCPs can change rules, aggressive haircuts create liquidity problems for members, creating political resistance.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a hidden risk in CCP collateral pools that can dwarf the benefit of holding collateral. During stress, CCPs may find their collateral pools have become highly correlated with member default risk through years of adverse selection, exactly when they need liquidity most.
common_traps: Assuming CCPs can simply 'reject risky collateral' without consequence
Thinking haircuts based on normal volatility capture WWR jump risk
Ignoring that members actively optimize collateral posting to their advantage
questions.real_world_example: During the Eurozone crisis, banks clearing with European CCPs would have strong incentives to post peripheral sovereign debt (Greek, Italian, Spanish) as IM rather than German Bunds, concentrating exactly the wrong-way risk in CCP collateral pools that would be liquidated at the worst possible prices if a member defaulted.

questions.question: What is the key difference between general wrong-way risk and specific wrong-way risk in counterparty credit exposure?
questions.answer_short: General WWR arises from macro-economic relationships (e.g., interest rates and default rates), while specific WWR comes from structural linkages between exposure/collateral and the counterparty's default (e.g., buying protection on a bank from that same bank).
questions.answer_long: General wrong-way risk is driven by broad economic factors and correlations that may be observable in historical data, such as the tendency for defaults to cluster during recessions when interest rates are low. Specific wrong-way risk arises from direct causal relationships between the transaction structure and the counterparty's creditworthiness, like posting own bonds as collateral or buying CDS protection from a related entity. General WWR can potentially be modeled using correlation approaches, while specific WWR often requires qualitative assessment and stress testing because it may be extreme and not captured by historical data.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction determines your modeling approach and risk management strategy. General WWR might be handled through correlation models and stress scenarios, while specific WWR often requires transaction-level controls, limits, or outright prohibition of certain structures.
common_traps: Assuming all WWR can be captured by historical correlation analysis
Treating specific WWR as if it were general WWR and applying inappropriate correlation models
Missing specific WWR because it hasn't appeared in historical data yet
questions.real_world_example: During the Asian crisis (1997-1998), dealers suffered heavy losses from FX forwards with Asian counterparties where both the currency weakened dramatically AND the counterparty defaulted simultaneously. This was specific WWR that historical correlations had underestimated.

questions.question: How does the CVA formula change when incorporating wrong-way risk, and what does the conditional exposure term represent?
questions.answer_short: CVA becomes: CVA = LGD × Σ EE(tᵢ | tᵢ = τc) × PD(tᵢ₋₁, tᵢ), where EE(tᵢ | tᵢ = τc) is the expected exposure conditional on counterparty default occurring at time tᵢ, replacing the unconditional EE.
questions.answer_long: In the presence of wrong-way risk, we must use conditional expected exposure: the expected exposure given that the counterparty defaults at that specific time. This replaces the unconditional expected exposure used in standard CVA calculations. The conditional exposure is typically higher than unconditional exposure in WWR situations because default occurs when exposure is elevated. The formula correctly captures the dependency between credit quality deterioration and exposure increases by conditioning the exposure calculation on the default event itself.
questions.why_it_matters: Using unconditional exposure when WWR exists systematically underestimates CVA, potentially by 50-100% or more. This leads to underpricing of trades, insufficient hedging, and inadequate capital allocation for counterparty risk.
common_traps: Continuing to use unconditional EE when WWR is present
Thinking correlation adjustments to unconditional EE are sufficient for strong WWR
Not recognizing that conditional EE must be recalculated, not just scaled
questions.real_world_example: A bank with receiver interest rate swaps to European sovereigns during 2010-2012 found that using unconditional EE dramatically underestimated CVA as sovereign spreads widened while swap values moved in-the-money simultaneously, creating 'cross-gamma' effects.

questions.question: A corporate client wants to enter a cross-currency swap receiving EUR and paying USD with a European bank. From the bank's perspective, explain the wrong-way risk and how it differs if the bank receives EUR instead.
questions.answer_short: If the bank pays EUR (receives USD), there's WWR: if the bank defaults, EUR likely weakens, increasing the bank's EUR payment obligation when it's least able to pay. If the bank receives EUR, this becomes right-way risk as EUR weakness reduces the bank's obligation.
questions.answer_long: When the bank pays EUR to the corporate, a default scenario would likely involve European financial stress causing both bank creditworthiness deterioration and EUR currency weakness. The EUR depreciation increases the value of the bank's USD receipts relative to its EUR payment obligations, making the trade more in-the-money to the corporate exactly when the bank defaults—classic wrong-way risk. If instead the bank receives EUR, currency weakness reduces what the counterparty owes the bank, creating favorable right-way risk. The cross-currency swap essentially represents a loan collateralized by the opposite currency, and if that collateral currency weakens dramatically, the effective collateral value diminishes.
questions.why_it_matters: Cross-currency swaps are major WWR products in bank portfolios. Proper identification determines whether CVA adjustments increase or decrease, affects pricing, and drives hedging strategy. The directionality matters enormously for capital allocation and risk limits.
common_traps: Not considering which currency you pay vs receive when assessing WWR direction
Assuming all cross-currency swaps have WWR regardless of direction
Forgetting that the counterparty location and currency relationship matter more than the currency pair alone
questions.real_world_example: During the European sovereign crisis (2010-2012), banks found that EUR cross-currency swaps where they paid EUR to non-European counterparties had significant WWR as EUR weakened alongside deteriorating bank credit quality, requiring major CVA increases.

questions.question: Why can historical correlation data be uninformative or misleading when trying to quantify wrong-way risk, particularly for specific WWR scenarios?
questions.answer_short: WWR is often subtle, extreme, and event-driven rather than continuous. Historical data may not contain the stress scenarios where WWR manifests, and zero observed correlation doesn't prove independence—there could be non-linear or jump dependencies.
questions.answer_long: Wrong-way risk presents several data challenges: First, extreme WWR events may be rare or unprecedented in the historical sample period (e.g., European sovereign defaults had no precedent before 2010). Second, the relationship may be non-linear or jump-to-default driven rather than continuous correlation, so standard correlation analysis misses the dependency. Third, WWR is often conditional on stress states that are underrepresented in normal market data. Fourth, the direction of causality may be unclear—does currency weakness cause defaults or vice versa? Finally, zero measured correlation between variables doesn't prove independence; there could be higher-moment dependencies or event-driven linkages that only appear in tail scenarios.
questions.why_it_matters: Over-reliance on historical correlation can create a false sense of security. Banks that trusted pre-crisis correlation data were blindsided by WWR losses in 2007-2009. Proper WWR assessment requires stress testing, scenario analysis, and qualitative judgment beyond just fitting correlations to historical time series.
common_traps: Trusting that zero historical correlation means no WWR exists
Using correlation measured in normal markets to predict crisis behavior
Not recognizing that WWR may be jump-driven rather than correlation-driven
Ignoring the direction of causality between exposure and default
questions.real_world_example: Before the 2010 European sovereign crisis, historical data showed little correlation between European sovereign credit spreads and EUR currency movements. However, when Greece faced default, this relationship changed dramatically, with implied residual EUR values dropping to 80-91% in quanto CDS quotes—a relationship invisible in pre-crisis data.

questions.question: Why does the hazard rate approach to modeling wrong-way risk typically generate only weak WWR effects even with high correlation parameters, and when is this approach most appropriate?
questions.answer_short: Hazard rate models generate continuous, gradual changes in credit spreads correlated with market variables. They miss jump-to-default effects and extreme dependencies, producing weak WWR even at 90% correlation. They're best for general WWR with observable continuous relationships.
questions.answer_long: The hazard rate approach models credit spread (hazard rate) as a stochastic process correlated with exposure-driving variables like interest rates or FX. While mathematically tractable and allowing direct calibration from observable time series, this approach has fundamental limitations. It assumes continuous, smooth evolution of credit quality and generates default as a gradual process. Real WWR often involves jumps, regime changes, or discontinuities at default. Even with 90% correlation, the approach generates modest CVA increases because defaults occur somewhat randomly along the credit spread path rather than at specific high-exposure moments. The method works best for general macro-driven WWR with observable historical relationships but fails to capture specific structural dependencies or jump effects.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the limitations prevents false confidence in WWR quantification. If you model FX-sovereign WWR using only hazard rates, you'll dramatically underestimate CVA because you miss the currency jump at default. Knowing when hazard rate approaches are insufficient helps you choose appropriate additional methods like jump models or stress scenarios.
common_traps: Thinking 90%+ correlation in hazard rate models captures all WWR
Using hazard rate approaches for specific WWR requiring jump models
Not supplementing continuous models with jump or stress scenarios
Believing tractability equals accuracy in WWR modeling
questions.real_world_example: Banks modeling interest rate swap WWR with sovereign counterparties using correlated hazard rates found the approach worked reasonably for gradual credit deterioration but completely missed the exposure spikes when sovereigns actually defaulted or were restructured, requiring additional jump-to-default scenarios.

questions.subtopic: Currency Jump and Residual Value Approach
questions.question: Using the residual value approach, explain how to estimate CVA on a 5-year FX forward with a BB-rated sovereign counterparty where you pay the local currency. How does this compare to a hazard rate approach?
questions.answer_short: Assume the currency jumps by (1 - RV) at default, where RV ≈ 41% for BB sovereigns from empirical data. This creates a floor on exposure at roughly 59% devaluation. Unlike hazard rate approaches, this produces time-homogeneous WWR effects and much larger CVA increases.
questions.answer_long: The residual value approach assumes that at the sovereign default time, the local currency experiences a discrete jump devaluation to some residual value. From Levy and Levin's empirical analysis, BB-rated sovereigns show an average 41% residual value, meaning a 59% devaluation at default. For your FX forward where you pay local currency, this devaluation creates immediate WWR: when the sovereign defaults, you owe more in USD-equivalent terms just as they're unable to pay. Unlike hazard rate models generating weak continuous effects, the jump approach creates a floor on conditional exposure—even with perfect collateralization pre-default, the jump cannot be collateralized within the margin period of risk. The CVA increase is substantial and relatively constant across maturities because the jump effect dominates. This approach is supported by CDS market quanto spreads showing significant discounts for local-currency protection versus USD protection.
questions.why_it_matters: The jump approach captures what hazard rate models miss: discontinuous FX moves at default. This is critical for proper pricing and risk management of sovereign FX trades. The difference can be 30-60% of the trade's CVA, directly impacting profitability and hedging requirements.
common_traps: Using the same RV for all maturities when early vs late defaults may differ
Assuming collateral eliminates WWR in jump scenarios (it doesn't)
Applying sovereign RV parameters to corporate counterparties without adjustment
Not validating RV assumptions against quanto CDS market prices
questions.real_world_example: During April 2011, the CDS market showed Italian sovereign protection was 30% cheaper in EUR vs USD (91 bps vs 131 bps for 5Y), implying a 69% residual EUR value on Italian default—validating the jump approach and providing direct market calibration for WWR models.

questions.question: In the structural approach to WWR, exposure distributions and default times are mapped to a bivariate distribution. What is the key advantage of this method, and what is its fundamental limitation in terms of parameter calibration?
questions.answer_short: Advantage: Pre-computed unconditional exposures can be reused, making it computationally efficient. Limitation: The correlation parameter between default time and exposure is abstract and opaque, making calibration difficult without clear economic intuition.
questions.answer_long: The structural approach's key innovation is separating exposure calculation from WWR incorporation. You first compute unconditional exposure distributions, then map these plus default time distributions onto a joint bivariate distribution (typically Gaussian). Positive dependency couples early defaults with high exposures. The computational efficiency is significant—no need to recalculate thousands of exposure paths. However, this efficiency comes with a major drawback: the correlation parameter linking default timing to exposure level lacks economic intuition. Unlike FX-credit correlations or interest rate-spread correlations which have observable market analogues, the default-time-to-exposure-level correlation is abstract. Calibration becomes problematic: what does 50% correlation actually mean economically? Should it be the same across counterparties? The parameter cannot be easily observed or validated, introducing significant model risk.
questions.why_it_matters: The structural approach is widely used in CVA systems because of its computational tractability when dealing with large portfolios. Understanding its calibration weakness is critical: you need robust sensitivity analysis, conservative parameter choices, and validation against other methods. The model's mathematical elegance shouldn't mask its parameter uncertainty.
common_traps: Treating the correlation parameter as if it has the same meaning as observable market correlations
Calibrating from limited historical default events without considering selection bias
Not stress-testing results across wide parameter ranges
Assuming the unconditional exposure distribution contains all relevant WWR information
questions.real_world_example: A major bank implemented structural WWR models across all counterparties using a standard 25% correlation. However, stress tests revealed this produced vastly different CVA impacts for sovereign vs corporate counterparties, leading them to abandon one-size-fits-all correlation and implement counterparty-type-specific parameters validated by senior risk committees.

questions.question: You're buying 5-year CDS protection on a reference entity with 250 bps spread from a counterparty with 500 bps spread (both LGD=60%). With 60% correlation between reference entity and counterparty defaults, what is the approximate fair premium you should pay, and why?
questions.answer_short: Approximately 200 bps instead of 250 bps. The 50 bps CVA (one-fifth of the risk-free premium) reflects that at 60% correlation, when the reference entity defaults and you need protection payment, there's significant probability the protection seller has also defaulted.
questions.answer_long: The severe WWR in CDS arises because the protection becomes valuable exactly when it's needed—at reference entity default. With 60% correlation, there's substantial probability of simultaneous or related defaults. From the chapter's model, the fair premium drops from 250 bps (risk-free) to roughly 200 bps, representing a massive 50 bps per annum CVA charge. At extreme 100% correlation, the premium falls to just above 100 bps (based on recovery value only, as the protection seller always defaults when protection is needed). This demonstrates why buying protection from systemically related counterparties is highly problematic. The WWR effect is asymmetric: selling protection shows much smaller CVA impact due to right-way risk—you owe money when the reference entity's spread tightens, which is when the protection buyer is less likely to default.
questions.why_it_matters: CDS WWR was central to monoline insurer failures in 2008-2009 and is critical for understanding CCP risk in CDS clearing. Banks that ignored this effect massively overvalued protection bought from related counterparties, creating hidden losses that materialized in the crisis. Proper CDS WWR pricing is essential for any credit derivatives business.
common_traps: Using standard CVA formulas designed for linear products on CDS
Ignoring the direction asymmetry (buying vs selling protection)
Not recognizing that even modest correlations create huge WWR in CDS
Assuming collateral fully mitigates CDS WWR (it often doesn't due to jumps)
questions.real_world_example: Banks that bought protection on subprime mortgages from monoline insurers in 2006-2007 priced it near par premium, ignoring WWR. When the housing market collapsed, the monolines' credit deteriorated alongside the reference obligations, and banks suffered massive CVA losses on protection that became nearly worthless due to counterparty default risk.

questions.question: Compare how collateral mitigates WWR in a structural correlation approach versus a currency jump approach. When is collateral most and least effective against WWR?
questions.answer_short: Structural approaches show collateral as highly effective (CVA becomes nearly insensitive to correlation) because exposure grows gradually and collateral can be called. Jump approaches show collateral as largely ineffective because discontinuous exposure increases cannot be collateralized within the margin period of risk.
questions.answer_long: This comparison reveals a fundamental tension in WWR modeling. In structural correlation models where exposure and default probability evolve continuously via correlated processes, collateral appears highly beneficial—as WWR increases (higher correlation), more collateral is typically held, substantially reducing conditional exposure. The CVA impact of correlation becomes muted. However, in jump-based approaches (like FX jump-to-default), collateral is nearly useless: the exposure increase is instantaneous at default and cannot be mitigated within the standard margin period of risk. The floor on exposure remains at the jump magnitude regardless of collateral terms. The truth likely lies between these extremes: collateral effectiveness depends on how gradually the WWR manifests. Systemic bank defaults may involve rapid exposure increases (jump-like), making collateral less effective, while corporate defaults might show more gradual deterioration (continuous), allowing collateral to help.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction determines whether you can rely on collateral to manage WWR or need additional controls. For sovereign FX trades, don't assume collateral solves the problem. For gradual macro-driven WWR, collateral may be a reasonable mitigant. The modeling approach choice has direct P&L impact through CVA calculations and capital requirements.
common_traps: Assuming all collateral equally mitigates WWR regardless of jump vs continuous dynamics
Using models that show collateral effectiveness when the underlying WWR is jump-driven
Not considering that systemic counterparties (who use collateral most) may have jump-like WWR
Ignoring margin period of risk extensions during stress events
questions.real_world_example: Banks with collateralized FX forwards to emerging market sovereigns found that while models predicted collateral would greatly reduce WWR, actual defaults (or near-defaults) involved such rapid currency moves that margin period of risk became extended (operational delays, legal disputes) and collateral proved far less effective than models suggested.

questions.question: Explain the paradox that CCPs face regarding WWR and credit quality of clearing members, and why this creates potential 'wrong-way margin' effects. How does the CCP waterfall resemble a CDO structure?
questions.answer_short: WWR increases with better credit quality (bigger surprise when they default), yet CCPs charge margins based on market risk not credit quality. Better-quality large banks present more systemic WWR but may pay lower margins. The CCP waterfall acts like a senior CDO tranche, heavily exposed to systemic risk.
questions.answer_long: CCPs face several interrelated WWR paradoxes. First, as shown empirically and theoretically, WWR effects are stronger for higher credit quality counterparties—their default is more unexpected and creates larger conditional exposures. Yet CCPs typically disassociate credit quality from initial margin, basing margins mainly on market risk. Second, the largest, highest-quality dealers are precisely the most systemically important, creating maximum WWR if they default. Third, the CCP waterfall structure resembles a CDO: defaulter-pays resources (initial margin, default fund contribution, CCP equity) form a first-loss piece, while remaining members have second-loss exposure through their default fund contributions and assessment rights. This second-loss position is like a senior CDO tranche—it only takes losses in systemic scenarios, making it highly concentrated in tail risk. The 'defaulter pays' layer must be thick enough that second-loss is rare, but this requires correctly pricing WWR into initial margins, which CCPs struggle to do.
questions.why_it_matters: This analysis explains why CCP risk may be more dangerous than commonly believed. If large systemically-important clearing members default (exact scenario with strongest WWR), CCP resources may prove inadequate, pushing losses onto surviving members through the waterfall. Understanding this helps evaluate whether central clearing actually reduces systemic risk or just concentrates it differently.
common_traps: Assuming CCPs have solved counterparty risk through margining
Not recognizing that better-credit members can present greater WWR
Treating CCP default fund contributions as fundamentally different from CDO tranches
Believing CCPs can avoid WWR by accepting only high-quality members (this may worsen systemic WWR)
questions.real_world_example: CDS CCPs face extreme WWR: if a major dealer defaults, it's likely during a credit crisis when CDS positions have maximum value and recovery on collateral (which may include credit-sensitive assets) is worst. The LCH.Clearnet default management in 2018 for a smaller energy member worked well, but questions remain about whether margins would be adequate for a Lehman-scale member default during a systemic crisis.
